newsitem.title: USA: SEC sues CS First Boston over Orange County bonds.
newsitem.headline: SEC sues CS First Boston over Orange County bonds.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission said Wednesday it sued CS First Boston Corp. and two of its former investment bankers for fraud in the sale of Orange County, Calif., bonds.
The move was the first SEC enforcement action against an investment firm involved in the county's ill-fated bond deals, which led to the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history.
SEC officials in Los Angeles said the lawsuit was part of the regulatory agency's ongoing investigation of the Orange County bankruptcy.

The regulatory agency said it was seeking permanent injunctions and unspecified civil penalties against the firm, a broker-dealer headquartered in New York, and two of its former investment bankers, Jerry Nowlin and Douglas Montague.
CS First Boston, a unit of CS Holding, a Swiss banking and financial services company, said there was no basis for the SEC's civil action against the firm.
"We believe that there is no basis for a fraud charge and we will defend the action vigorously," the firm said in a statement.
In the complaint, the SEC alleged fraud in the offer and sale of $110 million of Series B pension obligation bonds issued by Orange County in September 1994.

CS First Boston was the senior underwriter for about $320 million of pension obligation bonds issued by the county in September 1994. As underwriter, CS First Boston purchased the pension bonds from the county and sold them to investors.

The complaint alleged that, while participating in the drafting and preparing of the county's bond offering documents, CS First Boston and the two bankers "knew, or were reckless in not knowing, significant negative information about the county (investment) pools that was misrepresented in or omitted from the official statement."

The SEC said the firm knew or was "reckless in not knowing" about the county's use of risky derivative securities and that, as a result of rising interest rates during 1994, county investments had suffered significant market losses and collateral calls.

"To the contrary, CS First Boston, Nowlin, and Montague participated in the preparation of the official statement which cast the county pools in a false light by conveying the impression of safety and security," the SEC said.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy protection on Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June.
